name: Beta-propeller protein-associated neurodegeneration
aliases: Static encephalopathy of childhood with neurodegeneration in adulthood
static encephalopathy of childhood with neurodegeneration in adulthood

clinicalPearls: X-linked dominant disorder caused by de novo variants in WDR45; it predominantly affects females, and surviving affected males are often presumed to be somatic mosaics.

Characteristically biphasic: early-childhood global developmental delay, intellectual disability and epilepsy, followed after years of relative stability by an abrupt young-adult onset of progressive dystonia-parkinsonism and cognitive decline.
Formerly described as SENDA (static encephalopathy of childhood with neurodegeneration in adulthood), now recognised as the same WDR45 entity.

Rett-like features are common in the childhood phase (hand stereotypies, disordered sleep, poor speech development), so WDR45 testing is worthwhile in girls with a Rett-like picture and negative MECP2 testing.
In the neurodegenerative phase, iron accumulates in the substantia nigra and globus pallidus, with substantia nigra involvement often disproportionate.
A near-specific MRI clue is T1 hyperintensity of the substantia nigra and cerebral peduncles with a central band of hypointensity (a 'halo'), best appreciated alongside iron-sensitive sequences.
WDR45 encodes WIPI4, a seven-bladed beta-propeller scaffold protein essential to autophagosome formation, so BPAN is fundamentally a disorder of defective autophagy.
Adult-onset parkinsonism may respond to levodopa initially but is frequently complicated by early dyskinesias.
reference.pathophysiology: WDR45, located at Xp11.23, encodes WIPI4 (WD-repeat protein interacting with phosphoinositides 4), a member of a family of seven-bladed beta-propeller proteins that bind phosphatidylinositol-3-phosphate on the nascent phagophore membrane and coordinate elongation and maturation of the autophagosome during macroautophagy. Loss-of-function variants impair autophagic flux, so that damaged mitochondria, misfolded proteins and aberrant autophagic intermediates accumulate within neurons; over time this is accompanied by progressive deposition of iron in the basal ganglia and, characteristically, the substantia nigra. Because the gene is X-linked and almost all cases arise de novo, females predominate while hemizygous males typically survive only through somatic mosaicism, which also accounts for the phenotypic variability. The relatively static childhood encephalopathy reflects early developmental disruption, whereas the later abrupt neurodegenerative phase reflects failure of neuronal proteostasis and mitochondrial quality control in the nigrostriatal system.
additionalDifferentials: Rett syndrome (MECP2) and CDKL5-related developmental and epileptic encephalopathy
Other NBIA subtypes, particularly PKAN, MPAN and PLA2G6-associated neurodegeneration
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with iron-sensitive sequences (susceptibility-weighted or gradient-echo/T2*) plus T1 imaging to identify nigral and pallidal iron and the nigral 'halo'
WDR45 sequencing and deletion/duplication analysis, with consideration of testing for somatic mosaicism in males and mildly affected individuals
EEG to characterise the seizure disorder or epileptic encephalopathy
Serum caeruloplasmin and copper studies to exclude Wilson disease
Dopamine transporter (DAT) imaging, which may show a presynaptic dopaminergic deficit in the parkinsonian phase
redFlags: Abrupt cognitive regression or new dystonia-parkinsonism in a young adult with a previously static childhood encephalopathy
Rapidly worsening rigidity with swallowing difficulty and aspiration risk
Acute behavioural deterioration with loss of mobility
reference.prognosis: The childhood phase is relatively static, but the adult neurodegenerative phase brings progressive dystonia-parkinsonism, dementia and loss of independent mobility over years. No disease-modifying therapy exists and management is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Labelling the childhood phase as 'cerebral palsy' or non-specific intellectual disability and never testing WDR45.
Assuming an X-linked disorder must spare females or require a family history; in BPAN females predominate and de novo variants are the rule, so a negative family history does not exclude it.
Overlooking the diagnosis in Rett-like girls once MECP2 testing is negative.
Missing the nigral T1 hyperintensity because iron-sensitive and T1 sequences were not reviewed, especially as early MRI can be non-specific.
references: Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation (NBIA) clinical references
management: No disease-modifying therapy exists; management is supportive, with antiepileptic drugs selected for the childhood seizure disorder or epileptic encephalopathy
Symptomatic treatment of the later dystonia-parkinsonism with a trial of levodopa, and anticholinergics or focal botulinum toxin injections for troublesome dystonia
Address the early Rett-like phase with behavioural support, management of sleep disturbance and strategies for hand stereotypies
Multidisciplinary neurorehabilitation: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language and feeding support, and mobility aids as parkinsonism advances
Periodic neurological review with iron-sensitive MRI to track progression of nigral and pallidal iron accumulation and functional decline
Genetic counselling explaining the X-linked de novo WDR45 mechanism, with testing for parental or somatic mosaicism when recurrence risk is raised
Anticipatory and palliative care planning as independent mobility and cognition are progressively lost
